big_idea: Career reinvention doesn't require a dramatic leap into the unknown; it works better as a series of small, deliberate experiments launched from your existing strengths, which compound into meaningful change with far less risk than a single big bet.

tool.label: The Pivot Method (Plant, Scan, Pilot, Launch)
tool.text: Blake's four-stage method starts with Plant: taking stock of what's already working and defining what success looks like on a roughly one-year horizon. Scan maps the surrounding landscape of related people, skills, and roles. Pilot is the experimentation stage, designing small, low-risk tests to gather real evidence before committing. Launch means either fully committing or taking a 'little L' launch -- distilling what you learned into one or two next concrete steps. The method is cyclical, looping back through the four stages repeatedly.
tool.note: The method is oriented toward people who already have a stable base to pivot from, so it offers less concrete guidance for someone facing an involuntary, urgent transition like a layoff with no runway.

ideas.title: Double down before you jump
ideas.text: Blake argues the biggest pivot mistake is abandoning strengths too early; successful pivots amplify what's already working.

ideas.title: Small experiments beat big bets
ideas.text: Piloting cheap, reversible tests generates better information than committing fully to an unproven direction.

ideas.title: Your network is a scanning tool, not just a favor bank
ideas.text: Blake reframes networking as active research -- talking to people adjacent to a target role or industry.

ideas.title: Career change is a practice, not an event
ideas.text: The book treats pivoting as a repeatable skill to build over a career rather than a rare, high-stakes crisis.

ideas.title: Define success narrowly and near-term
ideas.text: Blake pushes readers to define what a successful pivot looks like within about a year, making progress measurable.

ideas.title: A little L launch still counts
ideas.text: Blake normalizes incremental, low-drama launches as legitimate pivot progress, not just dramatic career overhauls.

try_it: Write a one-page Plant audit this week: list what's currently working in your role and one measurable outcome you want in 12 months.
Identify three people doing adjacent work to a role you're curious about and schedule short conversations with them.
Design one low-cost pilot experiment you can start within two weeks to test a potential direction.
Set a recurring monthly review to reassess where you are in the Plant-Scan-Pilot-Launch cycle.
best_for: Professionals feeling stagnant in a stable job who want to explore a new direction without quitting first.
People early in a transition who want a structured, low-risk process rather than generic 'follow your passion' advice.
less_useful: Someone facing an urgent, involuntary transition who needs immediate tactical job-search help rather than an exploratory framework.
Readers who want hard data or longitudinal outcome studies on career-change success.

related.why: The Squiggly Career shares the same nonlinear, self-directed approach to career navigation.
The Career Manifesto offers a complementary purpose-first planning process for the same audience.
